The Hanseatic League was a confederation of merchant guilds and market towns spanning the Baltic Sea, the North Sea, and inland river systems, particularly the Elbe and Rhine, from the thirteenth to the seventeenth centuries. At its height in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, it encompassed nearly two hundred cities stretching from London to Novgorod, functioning as an economic network that bound northern Europe together through standardized weights, measures, legal codes, and trading privileges.

The League originated in the thirteenth century as an informal association of merchant communities in Baltic and North Sea coastal towns. Over time, it gradually formalized into a collective trading network unified by shared commercial interests. Its geography was centred on the Baltic and North Sea littoral, with major cities like Lübeck, Hamburg, Gdańsk—then called Danzig—and Bergen in Norway serving as its principal nodes, all connected by sea routes and inland rivers.

The League established warehouses known as kontore in foreign cities including London, Novgorod, Bergen, and Bruges, creating enclaves where Hanseatic merchants monopolized trade in essential goods like timber, furs, grain, fish, and amber. These merchants wielded extraordinary collective economic power, negotiating with kings and princes to guarantee trading rights, establish market monopolies, and even defend against piracy through their own merchant-organized fleets.

Standardized legal codes, weights, and measures made Hanseatic commercial law influential across northern Europe and served as a predecessor to modern commercial standardization. The League's power was remarkable—it rivalled kingdoms in influence and shaped the commercial networks that would eventually underpin the modern European economy. However, by the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, the League declined as nation-states centralized power, oceanic trade routes through the Atlantic and Indian Ocean overshadowed Baltic commerce, and rival trading powers from England, the Dutch territories, and Sweden emerged to challenge its dominance.
